rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Following al-Zamakhshari's reading through Sibawayh, the fa after a fronted object signals an understood condition, often after a command or prohibition semantically opposed to the following command.
rows.anchor: اعتبار الفاء مشعرة بشرط مقدر

rows.speaker: الأعشى
rows.claim: The poet's line illustrates an implied condition: if one worships anything, then worship God, with the fa marking the consequence.
rows.anchor: ولا تعبد الشيطان والله فاعبدا

rows.speaker: صاحب ( الكشاف )
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari lists emphases in ‘You alone, so fear Me’: the detached pronoun precedes the verb, its attached pronoun is repeated, fa adds force, and the wording implies a condition and repeated fear.
rows.anchor: عن صاحب ( الكشاف ) أنه قال : إن في قوله تعالى : { وإياي فارهبون } وجوها من التأكيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fronting expresses exclusivity, itself an intensifier, while repeating the subject in the attached pronoun reinforces predication; here the author ranks this phrasing among four increasingly emphatic patterns.
rows.anchor: في التعبير عن مثل هذا الاختصاص في كلام البلغاء مراتب أربع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In al-Zamakhshari's phrase ‘conjoined and conjoining,’ the terms mean what precedes and follows in ordinary language, not syntactic coordination, which would not work here.
rows.anchor: العطف اللغوي أي معقبا ومعقبا به لا العطف النحوي إذ لا يستقيم هنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most of the ten canonical readers omit the first-person yāʾ after the protective nūn in both connection and pause; Yaʿqūb retains it in both.
rows.anchor: وحذفت ياء المتكلم بعد نون الوقاية في قوله : { فارهبون } للجمهور من العشرة في الوصل والوقف وأثبتها يعقوب في الوصل والوقف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arab dialects differ: most omit the yāʾ only at pause, Hudhayl omits it in both positions, and Hijaz retains it in both.
rows.anchor: وجمهور العرب يحذفونها في الوقف دون الوصل وهذيل يحذفونها في الوقف والوصل وأهل الحجاز يثبتونها في الحالين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The majority's omission in connected reading follows the codex spelling and recitation; the verse ending is treated like pause, as Sibawayh says endings and rhyme permit deletion. Yaʿqūb follows Hijazi usage and his transmitted reading; the comparable non-final form keeps yāʾ in 2:186.
rows.anchor: لأن كلمة { فارهبون } كتبت في المصحف الإمام بدون ياء وقرئت كذلك في سنة القراءة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verse 2:44 is a parenthetical rebuke between the prayer-and-alms commands and the call to seek help: their prayer among worshippers does not suffice when they fail to practice the righteousness they teach.
rows.anchor: اعتراض بين قوله : { وأقيموا الصلاة } ( البقرة : 43 ) وقوله : { واستعينوا بالصبر والصلاة } ( البقرة : 45 )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The parenthesis lacks a coordinating waw to show that its central purpose is exposing their loss and corrupt state, not simply urging them to preach righteousness consistently.
rows.anchor: وللتنبيه على كونه اعتراضا لم يقرن بالواو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They teach and preach as artisans or merchants perform a trade, fulfilling religious duties for the ranks and salaries they expect, without examining their own conduct.
rows.anchor: كما يقوم الصانع بصناعته والتاجر بتجارته لا يقصدون إلا إيفاء وظائفهم الدينية حقها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The direct address grammatically covers all Israelites, implying each proclaims religious commands but does not obey them; alternatively, collective address can assign the rebuke to only the relevant subgroup, especially their scholars.
rows.anchor: والمخاطب بقوله : { أتأمرون } جميع بني إسرائيل الذين خوطبوا من قبل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Under the all-Israelite reading, ‘people’ may mean Arab polytheists, who listened when Jews recounted their religion; the Qur'an notes their former expectation of victory over unbelievers.
rows.anchor: فإن اليهود كانوا يذكرون لهم ما جاء به دينهم والعرب كانوا يحفلون بسماع أقوالهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, under the all-Israelite reading, ‘people’ means everyone besides the preacher, as in the idiom ‘do as people do’ and the Qur'anic example about people gathering against you.
rows.anchor: وإما أن يكون المراد من ( الناس ) من عدا الآمر كما تقول أفعل كما يفعل الناس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the address targets Israel's scholars, ‘people’ means ordinary Jewish followers whom the scholars command to righteousness while neglecting themselves.
rows.anchor: وعلى الوجه الثاني يكون المراد بالناس العامة من أمة اليهود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The scholars may also be tacitly accused of recognizing Islam's Messenger as truthful: they admonish followers but do not seek their own salvation.
rows.anchor: أو تعريض بأنهم يعلمون أن ما جاء به رسول الإسلام هو الحق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The address remains to the Israelites and teaches what will enable them to fulfill the commands and prohibitions just listed; after exhortation and warning, patience and prayer are the remedy for the drag of old habits.
rows.anchor: خطاب لبني إسرائيل بالإرشاد إلى ما يعينهم على التخلق بجميع ما عدد لهم من الأوامر والنواهي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Patience helps because attachment to familiar ways and weakness in leaving them impede peoples from following a sound religion; patience makes accepting truth easier.
rows.anchor: فإذا تدرعوا بالصبر سهل عليهم اتباع الحق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prayer here renews and strengthens the earlier command to establish prayer in 2:43, using confidence in the addressees as a subtle form of encouragement.
rows.anchor: فالمراد تأكد الأمر بها الذي في قوله : { وأقيموا الصلاة وآتوا الزكاة }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He rejects the view that ‘seek help’ shifts to Muslims: the conjunction signals continuity, and the following description of the humble as believers confirms the Israelite address.
rows.anchor: وهذا وهم لأن وجود حرف العطف ينادي على خلاف ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says it is no objection that unbelievers are being asked to use prayer: 2:43 likewise commands prayer and alms while addressing the Israelites.
rows.anchor: وقريب منه آنفا قوله تعالى : { وأقيموا الصلاة وآتوا الزكاة واركعوا مع الراكعين }

rows.speaker: الغزالي
rows.claim: Al-Ghazali defines religious patience as the steadfastness of the religious motive against the motive of appetite; the author finds this apt to the verse.
rows.anchor: ثبات باعث الدين في مقابلة باعث الشهوة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: More generally, patience is enduring and remaining steady through what displeases the self, whether for later good or reward, or because escape is impossible, while avoiding panic and vexation.
rows.anchor: فالصبر احتمال وثبات على ما لا يلائم

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: A report in the Ṣaḥīḥ says that true, complete patience occurs at the first shock; the author explains this as patience before one knows escape is impossible, while later calm acceptance is still real patience.
rows.anchor: ورد في ( الصحيح ) : ( إنما الصبر عند الصدمة الأولى )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prayer here means the Islamic ritual as a comprehensive act of praising God in speech, deed, and belief; thus the two means of help are patience and gratitude.
rows.anchor: وهي مجموع محامد لله تعالى ، قولا وعملا واعتقادا

rows.speaker: الغزالي
rows.claim: Al-Ghazali says faith is half patience and half gratitude; the author calls this a good observation.
rows.anchor: وقد قيل إن الإيمان نصفه صبر ونصفه شكر كما في ( الإحياء )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Patience underlies the virtues because moral excellence depends on strong will and restraining appetite and anger; for example, forbearance, generosity, learning, piety, courage, justice, and work all involve patience.
rows.anchor: فما التحلم والتكرم والتعلم والتقوى والشجاعة والعدل والعمل في الأرض ونحوها إلا من ضروب الصبر

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: A saying attributed to Ali captures the point that courage is patience for an hour.
rows.anchor: ومما يؤثر عن علي رضي الله عنه : الشجاعة صبر ساعة

rows.speaker: زفر بن الحارث الكلابي
rows.claim: Zufar ibn al-Harith al-Kilabi excuses his people's retreat by saying their opponents proved more patient in facing death.
rows.anchor: ولكنهم كانوا على الموت أصبرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qur'an 103:1–3 makes patience complete the means of success; the Qur'an also links patience with leadership, Israel's favor, and divine companionship, as the author notes through al-Ghazali.
rows.anchor: وحسبك بمزية الصبر أن الله جعله مكمل سبب الفوز

rows.speaker: الغزالي
rows.claim: Al-Ghazali says the Qur'an mentions patience in more than seventy places, associates most good and ranks with it, and makes it their fruit.
rows.anchor: ذكر الله الصبر في القرآن في نيف وسبعين موضعا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Faith itself entails patience: accepting what lies beyond sense, obeying a human messenger, and departing from inherited religions oppose the self's habits; patience makes these duties easier for truth's sake.
rows.anchor: فإن فيه مخالفة النفس هواها ومألوفها في التصديق بما هو مغيب عن الحس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Commentators differ over ‘it is difficult’: some take the pronoun as prayer, which burdens the self; another takes it as seeking help through patience and prayer, by analogy with 5:8; al-Zamakhshari allows it to refer to all commands from 2:40 through 2:45.
rows.anchor: اختلف المفسرون في معاد ضمير { إنها } فقيل عائد إلى الصلاة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author prefers the broadest antecedent, all the preceding commands, as the clearest and most inclusive reading; he considers all these referents intended.
rows.anchor: وهذا أوضح الأقوال وأجمعها والمحامل مرادة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Great’ means difficult or burdensome here, a familiar metaphor because hardship accompanies carrying or achieving something great; Qur'anic parallels use the same sense.
rows.anchor: والمراد بالكبيرة هنا الصعبة التي تشق على النفوس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khushūʿ literally denotes shrinking or lowering; al-Nābigha's ‘a low, worn water-trough rim’ illustrates the loss of height, while submission is another form of lowering.
rows.anchor: والخشوع لغة هو الانزواء والانخفاض

rows.speaker: جعفر بن عبلة الحارثي
rows.claim: Jaʿfar ibn ʿAblah's verse uses ‘I humbled myself’ in the sense of submitting; the author explains inward humility as stillness and restraint from refusal or disobedience.
rows.anchor: فلا تحسبي أني تخشعت بعدكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The humble here discipline and tame the self, train it to rest in God's command and seek good outcomes, and avoid being deceived by immediate desire; such a soul is ready to receive good.
rows.anchor: والمراد بالخاشع هنا الذي ذلل نفسه وكسر سورتها وعودها أن تطمئن إلى أمر الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The humble may be understood as those who fear and consider future consequences; patience's restraint and prayer's fixed times then become easier despite competing desires, work, or pleasure.
rows.anchor: وكأن المراد بالخاشعين هنا الخائفون الناظرون في العواقب

rows.speaker: كثير
rows.claim: Kathīr's verse illustrates that when the self is prepared for an affliction, it becomes submissive to it.
rows.anchor: إذا وطنت يوما لها النفس ذلت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Many laws aim to train this disposition, with fasting the greatest example.
rows.anchor: وأحسب أن مشروعية أحكام كثيرة قصد الشارع منها هذا المعنى وأعظمها الصوم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He rejects restricting humility to the inward reverence of standing in prayer described by Ibn Rushd: that is a feature of prayer and the worshipper's excellence, so it cannot explain why prayer is easier for the one told to seek help through prayer.
rows.anchor: ولا يصح حمل الخشوع هنا على خصوص الخشوع في الصلاة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clause about expecting to meet God explains the humble and shows the source of their humility; ‘expect’ means firm conviction here, since Arabic often uses ẓann for certainty.
rows.anchor: فدل على أن المراد من الظن هنا الإعتقاد الجازم وإطلاق الظن في كلام العرب على معنى اليقين كثير جدا

rows.speaker: أوس بن حجر
rows.claim: Aws ibn Ḥajar's ‘certain in his expectation’ shows ẓann can mean certainty, not merely probability.
rows.anchor: فأرسله مستيقن الظن أنه

rows.speaker: دريد بن الصمة
rows.claim: Durayd ibn al-Ṣimmah likewise uses ẓann for a confident belief about two thousand armored men; the word can signify either certain or probable belief.
rows.anchor: فقلت لهم ظنوا بألفي مدجج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Meeting God and returning to Him are metaphors for resurrection and judgment, or for vision and reward, since bodily meeting and return to a place one left are impossible here.
rows.anchor: والملاقاة والرجوع هنا مجازان عن الحساب والحشر أو عن الرؤية والثواب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage indirectly praises Muslims and urges the Israelites to emulate believers; if the address instead shifts to Muslims, it indirectly censures Jews and hypocrites.
rows.anchor: والمقصود من قوله : { وإنها لكبيرة } إلخ التعريض بالثناء على المسلمين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mulaqāt derives from laqiya, meeting as presence; here it means appearing before God for judgment and thus believing in resurrection, as in the earlier Adam passage and later references.
rows.anchor: واللقاء الحضور كما تقدم في قوله : { فتلقى آدم من ربه كلمات }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The vocative renews the address to Israel to stress this appeal. Their remembered favors are only a brief prelude, since eloquence moves promptly to the central demand and signals its urgency.
rows.anchor: أعيد خطاب بني إسرائيل بطريق النداء مماثلا لما وقع في خطابهم الأول لقصد التكرير للاهتمام بهذا الخطاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The narration shifts from addressing Israel to speaking about them to make their example instructive and imply they persist in error without admitting their wrongdoing; the wrong was their weariness with manna and quail, later recalled in 2:61.
rows.anchor: وغير الأسلوب في هذه الجملة إذ انتقل من خطاب بني إسرائيل إلى الحديث عنهم بضمير الغيبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘They did not wrong Us’ anticipates the later complaint about their ingratitude for God's provision, hastening judgment that their character had not softened despite warnings and favors.
rows.anchor: فكان قوله : { وما ظلمونا } تمهيدا له وتعجيلا بتسجيل قلة شكرهم على نعم الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In ‘they wronged only themselves,’ fronting ‘themselves’ marks restriction; negation followed by affirmation already creates it, and the fronting reinforces the emphasis, like an ignorant person acting as his own enemy.
rows.anchor: قدم فيه المفعول للقصر وقد حصل القصر أولا بمجرد الجمع بين النفي والإثبات ثم أكد بالتقديم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A poem about reaching Khurasan and then returning illustrates concise ellipsis: if return follows arrival, saying ‘we reached Khurasan’ can itself mean that it is time to return.
rows.anchor: ثم القفول فقد جئنا خراسانا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A fa is ‘explanatory’ only when the following clause cannot coordinate naturally with what precedes; otherwise it is a conjunction, with any omitted material simply concise ellipsis.
rows.anchor: أن الفاء لا تعد فاء فصيحة إلا إذا لم يستقم عطف ما بعدها على ما قبلها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The water's gushing follows directly from God's command to Moses to strike the rock: Moses would obey, and a petitioner told how to act knows the requested outcome follows, as when a pupil is told to open a specified chapter.
rows.anchor: لأن الانفجار مترتب على قوله تعالى لموسى : { اضرب بعصاك الحجر }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He rejects al-Zamakhshari's reconstruction of an implicit conditional—‘if you strike, then water gushes’—as unclear; he says the command and result coordinate directly.
rows.anchor: ومن العجب ذكره في ( الكشاف )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command ‘go down to a town’ is a comparable case where the intended relation is clear without inventing an implicit condition.
rows.anchor: ومنه قوله تعالى الآتي : { اهبطوا مصرا }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This sentence continues the preceding pattern of recounting God's favors, whether pure favors or favors mixed with ingratitude and subsequent pardon, so its content should also be a favor.
rows.anchor: فالظاهر أن يكون مضمون هذه الجملة نعمة أيضا

rows.speaker: الفخر
rows.claim: Al-Fakhr's reading treats ‘go down to Egypt, and you will have what you asked’ as God's answer and therefore a favor, even though it is conditional on entering a town.
rows.anchor: فيؤخذ من كلام الفخر أن قوله تعالى : { اهبطوا مصرا فإن لكم ما سألتم } هو كالإجابة لما طلبوه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author finds al-Fakhr's proposed favor very remote because the text never establishes that they actually received the food they requested.
rows.anchor: ولا يخفى أنه بعيدجدا لأن إعطاءهم ما سألوه لم يثبت وقوعه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A reading transmitted through al-Fakhr and explained by ʿAbd al-Ḥakīm says asking to replace manna and quail was sinful ingratitude: ‘patience’ implies dislike, and the rebuke confirms it; the favor was pardon and the concession to go down.
rows.anchor: ويؤخذ من كلام المفسرين الذي صدر الفخر بنقله ووجهه عبد الحكيم أن سؤالهم تعويض المن والسلوى بالبقل ونحوه معصية

rows.speaker: الفخر
rows.claim: Al-Fakhr holds that requesting another blessing for a known purpose is not itself disobedience.
rows.anchor: لأن طلب الانتقال من نعمة لغيرها لغرض معروف لا يعد معصية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects the sin-and-pardon interpretation as weak: ‘go down’ grants no favor, and the request gives no evidence of sin, since asking to move from one favor to another for a familiar purpose is not disobedience.
rows.anchor: ولا يخفى أن هذا بعيد إذ ليس في قوله { اهبطوا } إنعام عليهم ولا في سؤالهم ما يدل على أنهم عصوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The episode shifts from favors to Israel's poor choice of appetite, which may still be lawful, but their words show discourtesy toward Moses and the benefactor: ‘we cannot endure’ casts the given food as hateful.
rows.anchor: مع ما في صيغة طلبهم من الجفاء وقلة الأدب مع الرسول ومع المنعم إذ قالوا : { لن نصبر }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author reads lan as extending negation throughout every time of ‘endure’: they announce they will no longer eat manna and quail, pressuring Moses to ask at once and implying they have made acceptance impossible.
rows.anchor: فإن ( لن ) تدل على استغراق النفي لأزمنة فعل { نصبر } من أولها إلى آخرها وهو معنى التأبيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's answer withdraws special care: instead of providing food, water, and shade as before, He orders them to go to a town and procure their own, a disciplinary rebuke for their attitude rather than punishment for a sinful request.
rows.anchor: فكان جواب الله لهم في هذه الطلبة أن قطع عنايته بهم وأهملهم ووكلهم إلى نفوسهم

rows.speaker: ابن عطاء الله
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭāʾ Allāh warns that a seeker may misread delayed punishment as approval; God may quietly withdraw spiritual provision or leave the seeker to personal desires, placing the person at a distance without awareness.
rows.anchor: من جهل المريد أن يسيء الأدب فتؤخر العقوبة عنه فيقول لو كان في هذا إساءة لعوقبت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Worldly deprivation and loss of spiritual gifts are not consequences of a legal sin under divine command; they resemble causal ordering in the world's system. Only afterlife punishment proves the act was sinful, resolving the interpretive difficulty.
rows.anchor: ولكنها من أشباه خطاب الوضع ترجع إلى ترتب المسببات على أسبابها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse alludes to the Torah's account: after leaving Sinai/Horeb for Paran in year two and traveling toward Hebron, Israelites remembered free fish and produce in Egypt, complained about manna, and wept; God was angered, Moses sought pardon, and God sent quail, which they stored for a month.
rows.anchor: وقد أشارت الآية إلى قصة ذكرتها التوراة مجملة منتثرة
